strengths: Addresses an underexplored but practically important dimension—efficiency (number of retrievals) in RAG systems alongside traditional accuracy metrics
Achieves strong empirical results with 100x reduction in training data: 78.77% recall on HotPotQA (3B model, 1K examples) vs. LeReT's 77.10% (8B model, 90K examples)
Valuable baseline contribution: ReAct with optimized prompts proves highly competitive, challenging claims about necessity of large-scale fine-tuning
Well-motivated two-stage design with clear insight that learning exploration vs. stopping can conflict in single-stage training; clean separation improves learning signals
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three datasets (HotPotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue) with multiple metrics (recall, F1, EM, efficiency) and meaningful ablations
Practical efficiency gains: ~53% reduction in searches on HotPotQA while improving F1 by +3.5%
Strong reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, training procedures, clear dataset descriptions, and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Stage 1 applies standard supervised fine-tuning; Stage 2 uses standard GRPO without algorithmic innovation; reward function is relatively straightforward

Incomplete/inconsistent baseline comparisons: SearchR1 and CoRAG results missing or incomplete in main tables; different retrievers/models (E5 vs. ColBERT, KILT vs. Wikipedia) used for recent method comparisons; CoRAG comparison lacks answer-level metrics
Design choices lack justification: 90/10 FINISH split appears arbitrary without ablation; budget B=6 not justified; reward hyperparameters (Rmax, α, τ) selected without sensitivity analysis
Circular reward design: h* (optimal stopping point) defined relative to FRUGALRAG-Explore policy itself, creating potential bias toward reference policy

Off-the-shelf answer generator significantly limits performance (acknowledged): notable gap on 2WikiMultiHopQA (36.13 vs. 41.40 EM vs. Search-R1); joint training not explored despite being mentioned as limitation
Generalization not evaluated: limited to Wikipedia-based QA only; unclear if efficiency gains transfer to other domains or retrieval sources
No statistical significance testing: results appear single-run without error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple random seeds, making it difficult to assess if differences are meaningful
Limited failure analysis: no investigation of question types requiring more/fewer searches, when model stops too early, or which types benefit most from adaptive retrieval
Prompt optimization dependency: ReAct FS baseline depends on 50-example prompt optimization; cost-benefit relative to 1000-example fine-tuning not clearly analyzed

strengths: Addresses practical and understudied problem of inference-time efficiency in multi-hop RAG systems
Demonstrates that optimized ReAct few-shot prompting is surprisingly competitive with large-scale fine-tuning methods (useful empirical finding challenging recent claims)
Comprehensive evaluation across three standard benchmarks (HotPotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue) with multiple metrics
Evaluation across multiple model sizes (3B, 7B, 8B Instruct models) shows some generality
Achieves substantial reduction in inference-time search operations (~50%) while maintaining competitive performance
Clear two-stage framework design with intuitive motivation for separating exploration from stopping decisions
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Stage 1 is standard SFT, Stage 2 directly applies existing GRPO; the two-stage design addresses instability but lacks conceptual contribution

Incomplete and unfair baseline comparisons: LeReT, Search-R1 results mostly incomplete or missing; different answer generators (off-the-shelf vs. trained) used across methods; CoRAG comparison uses different retriever/index

Overstated data efficiency claims: actual cost includes 50-example prompt optimization dataset, n=4 bootstrapped prompt generation, multiple rollout generation and selection—true data efficiency understated
No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported; missing error analysis and failure case discussion

Reward function design lacks justification: circular definition of h* relative to FRUGALRAG-Explore, no ablation on hyperparameters (R_max, α, τ), no analysis of reward-metric mismatch (training on recall vs. evaluating on answer quality)

Incomplete evaluation rigor: FRUGALRAG-SFT performs comparably to full RL on Qwen2.5-7B (Fig 2) but this important finding unexplained; no generalization to out-of-domain settings; no computational cost or wall-clock latency comparisons
Efficiency definition incomplete: optimizes for search count but ignores context length growth, retriever encoding time, and total end-to-end latency
Presentation issues: broken table references ('Table ??'), difficult-to-read figures, key implementation details scattered or in appendix
Missing critical analysis: no sensitivity analysis for reward hyperparameters, no investigation of when/why adaptive budgets outperform fixed budgets, no visualization of learned stopping behavior

strengths: Addresses important and overlooked problem of efficiency in RAG; clear motivation that inference latency matters
Strong empirical results across three diverse benchmarks (HotPotQA, 2Wiki, MuSiQue) achieving 100x reduction in training data (1000 vs 90K-100K examples)
Provides valuable methodological insight: ReAct with few-shot optimization is a stronger baseline than typically acknowledged in literature
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple model sizes (3B, 7B, 8B), diverse metrics (Recall, Support F1, F1, EM, Match), ablation studies, and adaptive vs fixed budget analysis
Well-motivated two-stage design with clear rationale for decoupling exploration from stopping decisions
Detailed experimental specifications and reproducibility documentation with promised code release
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—primarily combines existing techniques (ReAct, supervised fine-tuning, GRPO) without significant algorithmic innovation; reward function is straightforward

Incomplete and problematic baseline comparisons: different retrievers (ColBERT vs E5), model sizes, and training data across baselines makes fair attribution difficult; authors acknowledge comparisons are not directly comparable
Significant architectural limitation: uses off-the-shelf answer generator rather than training jointly, causing acknowledged performance gaps vs Search-R1 especially on 2Wiki
Circular definition of optimal rollout length h*: defined relative to FrugalRAG-Explore's performance, creating dependency on reference policy rather than ground truth
Reward function design lacks justification: multiple hyperparameters (Rmax, α, τ) with no sensitivity analysis, arbitrary logarithmic penalty function, unjustified 90/10 FINISH ratio
Generalization concerns: all datasets are Wikipedia-based, 1000 training examples from same domain as test set, no out-of-domain evaluation despite acknowledged limitations

Multi-stage training complexity not fully acknowledged: requires prompt optimization (50 examples), bootstrapped dataset generation, supervised fine-tuning, and RL fine-tuning—still requires domain-specific ground truth documents
Missing critical analyses: no human evaluation, no failure case analysis, no study of question type effects, Figure 1a's 'estimated optimal searches' lacks noise/reliability discussion
Risk of data distribution mismatch: 7B-Instruct models generate dataset for 3B fine-tuning; unclear if 3B overfits to 7B patterns, potentially explaining strong 3B results
% Tradeoff metrics introduced without sufficient justification for why these specific metric combinations (F1+EM+Match)/3×Searches represent the right optimization target

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation with clear insight that RL should optimize stopping rather than increase search steps
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (HotPotQA, 2Wiki, MuSiQue, BrowseCompPlus), retrievers, and answer generators with extensive ablations
Significant practical benefit: achieves competitive performance with only 1,000 training examples (100× reduction) compared to existing methods
Strong evidence of adaptive behavior with demonstrated correlations (r=0.82-0.95) between question difficulty and number of searches (Table 4)
Thorough analytical work including comparisons with heuristic stopping rules, cross-dataset robustness testing, and detailed ablation studies
Zero-shot generalization to harder datasets (BrowseCompPlus) demonstrates potential for out-of-domain transfer
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: straightforward application of SFT followed by RL with hand-crafted reward; two-stage approach is intuitive but not innovative

Unclear contribution of Stage-2 RL: performance on HotPotQA (E5) shows no change in recall (70.40%) or searches (2.89) after RL stage compared to Stage-1 alone, suggesting primary benefits come from exploration not optimization
Modest absolute performance improvements: marginal MBE gains over CoRAG (58.5% vs 58.2% on HotPotQA), with CoRAG achieving better results on 2Wiki and MuSiQue when using standard metrics

Training requires ground truth documents for recall computation in Stage-1 (Algorithm 1, line 18) to select best trajectories, limiting real-world applicability despite claims of not requiring final answer annotations

Reward function design issues: definition of optimal h* is somewhat circular (depends on τ which is set based on base policy); limited justification for logarithmic penalty form; insufficient sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters (τ, α, Rmax)

Incomplete baseline comparisons: strong ReAct Few-Shot baseline (79.6% recall) suggests significant gains may come from exploration rather than RL; different training data sizes and generators used across comparisons
Main results lack confidence intervals and statistical significance testing; only appendix (Table D) reports standard deviations
Missing analysis of why Stage-2 RL provides improvements when it does, and failure mode analysis (e.g., when optimal stopping is ill-defined)

strengths: Practical motivation: Addresses real efficiency concerns in RAG systems with sensible approach to adaptive test-time compute
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (HotPotQA, 2Wiki, MuSiQue, BrowseCompPlus), retrievers, and answer generators
Extensive ablations including budget sensitivity, training data scaling, model agnosticity, reward design, and comparisons with heuristics
Clear documentation of efficiency-accuracy tradeoffs with consistent ~50% reduction in search operations
Good empirical analysis showing adaptive scaling with question difficulty (high correlation: r=0.82-0.95 in Table 4)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Combines standard supervised finetuning (on bootstrapped data) with existing GRPO algorithm. Core claim that joint optimization of coverage/efficiency causes instability is unsupported by evidence

Overclaimed two-stage necessity: Table 7 shows Stage-2-without-Stage-1 achieves 66.5% vs 70.4% recall, but paper provides no analysis of why joint training fails or whether this reflects optimization difficulty rather than fundamental limitation

Data efficiency claims misleading: 1,000 examples are same as compared baselines; recent work achieves comparable results with 871-1440 examples (Table 2). The '100× reduction' headline cherry-picks against highest-data methods

Inconsistent metric improvements: CoRAG outperforms on 2Wiki/MuSiQue MBE (59.0% vs 50.4%, 40.5% vs 36.4% respectively with E5). Claims of state-of-the-art are selective; search efficiency advantage doesn't offset lower accuracy

Ad-hoc reward design: Piecewise function in Eq. 1 contains multiple hyperparameters (Rmax, α, τ) with limited justification. Removing late-stop penalty (Table 8) yields similar recall (70.5%) but more searches (3.144), suggesting design trades rather than fundamental principle

Weak generalization evidence: BrowseCompPlus shows low absolute performance (20.46%); comparison with DeepSeek-R1 (16.39%) lacks controlled training procedures. Model 'adaptation' to larger budgets may reflect test-time search effectiveness rather than sophisticated learning

Evaluation concerns: MBE metric depends on Qwen3-32B evaluator without sensitivity analysis. No confidence intervals on main results; Appendix D shows std ~±1.21. Marginal improvements (e.g., 61.4% vs 58.2% CoRAG on HotPotQA) fall within noise

Circular train-test dependency: Optimal stopping point h* determined from ground-truth evidence unavailable at test time, encouraging overfitting to training distributions rather than learning generalizable stopping criteria
RL stability unclear: Only 400 training steps; convergence not verified. Choice of GRPO over PPO unexplained. Reproducibility limited by single checkpoint selection (final) and GPU requirements

Limited scope: Only Wikipedia-based open-domain QA. No domain adaptation analysis despite significant cross-dataset performance degradation (Table 14: trained on HotPotQA, 60.4% recall on 2Wiki vs 58.8% in-domain)

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear practical contributions: achieves competitive performance with only 1,000 training examples (100× reduction vs. prior work) while reducing retrieval costs by ~50%
Sound framework design validated through ablations: two-stage separation is justified by showing joint optimization is unstable (Tables 7-8)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple datasets, retrievers, answer generators, 14+ baselines, extensive ablations including budget sensitivity, sample count analysis, and cross-dataset generalization

Adaptive query allocation validated quantitatively: strong correlations (r=0.82-0.95) between question difficulty and search count, demonstrating the model learns difficulty-based computation allocation
Clear modularity and interpretability: using off-the-shelf answer generators isolates retrieval improvements from generation gains, strengthening claims
Excellent efficiency-accuracy tradeoff analysis: Figure 1 and Table 5 clearly demonstrate ~50% search reduction while maintaining or improving answer quality on HotPotQA
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Stage 1 uses standard supervised finetuning with bootstrapping, Stage 2 applies existing GRPO algorithm off-the-shelf; main contribution is their combination with a straightforward reward function

Circular definition of optimal stopping criterion: h* is defined as 'minimum hop where recall ≥ τ' but τ is set based on FRUGALRAG-Explore's performance, creating circularity that lacks justification. Why should the exploration policy define the stopping target?

Modest improvements on standard metrics: On HotPotQA E5 (58.5% vs 58.2% CoRAG), underperforms on 2WikiMultiHopQA (50.4% vs 59.0%) and MuSiQue (36.4% vs 40.5%), with main advantage being efficiency rather than accuracy

Reward function hyperparameter sensitivity under-explored: Multiple hyperparameters (τ, α, Rmax, 90-10 split) appear arbitrary; limited sensitivity analysis beyond budget B; design choices like Rmax=2.0 'for stability' lack principled motivation

Unfair efficiency comparisons: CoRAG trained on >100k examples with joint generator training; different data scales make direct comparison problematic. Custom 'Efficiency Tradeoff' metric may favor efficiency-focused methods. Token/FLOP analysis (Tables 10-12) shows FrugalRAG often uses comparable or higher compute
Insufficient statistical rigor: Only 3 RL training runs reported; standard deviations overlap with some baselines; no formal significance testing. No convergence analysis despite 400 training steps

BrowseCompPlus comparisons are misleading: Comparing 7B model against 600B, 120B, and 32B models with different optimization objectives; large baseline variance (oss-120b-low: 25.54% vs oss-20b-high: 35.06%) makes 20-21% accuracy gains difficult to interpret
Incomplete failure analysis: Only 3 qualitative examples (Table 15); no investigation of when early stopping fails or precision-recall tradeoffs; limited error analysis across datasets

Cross-dataset generalization concerns: Non-trivial performance drops when training on one dataset and testing on another (e.g., HotPotQA→MuSiQue: recall 69.1→53.3); limited investigation of dataset-specific factors

Training complexity under-acknowledged: Requires 8 H100 GPUs for Stage 1 + 7 H100 GPUs for Stage 2 (expensive); prompt optimization overhead not reflected in '1000 examples' claim; cost-benefit vs. simply scaling models is absent
